\chapter{Asking Nicely}
\label{ch:hi-asking-nicely}
\hlchaptermodality{65}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for something in Hindi with the courtesy word the occasion asks for.}

Complete HI-C65-manners and say all five words in order.

\section[mehrabānī]{\hi{मेहरबानी} (mehrabānī) — kindness}

\label{lesson:HI-C65-kindness}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{zyādā} mean, and what did \emph{kam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मेहरबानी}}
\textbf{\hi{मेहरबानी}} (\emph{mehrabānī}) — \textquotedblleft{}kindness\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \emph{mihrbān}, 'kind', with the quality-ending on the back of it. Under \emph{mihrbān} is \emph{mihr}, an old Iranian word for love and for the sun, and the god Mithra before either.

Two words in your Hindi now begin \emph{meh-} and are not related at all: \hi{मेहमान}, the guest, is Persian \emph{mihmān}, a different word entirely. Same opening syllable in our letters, separate families.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for asking well.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mehrabānī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mehrabānī}, then \emph{mehmān}, and say which one is the guest
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{मेहरबानी} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}kindness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vintī]{\hi{विनती} (vintī) — an entreaty}

\label{lesson:HI-C65-entreaty}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mehrabānī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{विनती}}
\textbf{\hi{विनती}} (\emph{vintī}) — \textquotedblleft{}an entreaty\textquotedblright{}.

Usually derived from Sanskrit \hi{विज्ञप्ति} (\emph{vijñapti}), 'a respectful making-known', which is what a petition to a king was called. The heavy conjunct in the middle collapsed on its way through Prakrit and left \hi{विनती}.

It sits above \hi{कृपया} in weight. \hi{कृपया} goes in front of a request the way 'please' does; \hi{विनती} is the request itself, offered from below, and it turns up in prayer and in a plea as often as in ordinary speech.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vintī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vintī}, then \emph{kṛpayā}, and say which one is the asking itself
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{विनती} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}an entreaty\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anumati]{\hi{अनुमति} (anumati) — permission}

\label{lesson:HI-C65-permission}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vintī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{अनुमति}}
\textbf{\hi{अनुमति}} (\emph{anumati}) — \textquotedblleft{}permission\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit, and transparent: \hi{अनु} (\emph{anu}), 'along with, after', plus \hi{मति} (\emph{mati}), 'thought'. Permission is thinking along with someone — agreeing in mind before agreeing in words.

It is the formal one. On a form, at a desk, or in front of anyone whose yes carries weight, \hi{अनुमति} is the word; among friends nobody says it. Hindi keeps a Sanskrit word in reserve for exactly these rooms.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{anumati}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{anumati}, then \emph{dhanyavād}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{अनुमति} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}permission\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bharosā]{\hi{भरोसा} (bharosā) — trust}

\label{lesson:HI-C65-trust}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{anumati} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{भरोसा}}
\textbf{\hi{भरोसा}} (\emph{bharosā}) — \textquotedblleft{}trust\textquotedblright{}.

Usually built on \hi{भर} (\emph{bhara}), 'a load, a support', from the root \hi{भृ} (\emph{bhṛ-}), 'to bear, to carry'. Trust is named as the thing that takes your weight.

That picture runs through the way the word is said, too: a speaker puts \hi{भरोसा} on someone rather than in them. The load goes on top, and the person underneath either holds or does not.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bharosā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bharosā}, then \emph{dost}, and say who takes the weight
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{भरोसा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}trust\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[adab]{\hi{अदब} (adab) — good manners}

\label{lesson:HI-C65-manners}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{अदब}}
\textbf{\hi{अदब}} (\emph{adab}) — \textquotedblleft{}good manners\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \emph{adab}, and here is the surprise: the same word means literature. Courtesy and letters were one idea — the cultivation that makes a person fit company, whether it shows in a bow or on a page.

Guard it against \hi{आदर}, which you already own. \emph{ādar} is respect you feel and show upward; \emph{adab} is the whole trained manner a person carries. Close in our letters, and not the same word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \hi{मेहरबानी}, \hi{विनती}, \hi{अनुमति}, \hi{भरोसा}, \hi{अदब}. Enough to ask for a thing at the weight the room asks for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{adab}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{dhanyavād}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{अदब} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}good manners\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
